recent_posts.title: Overly complex C++ substring check that reinvents string::find
recent_posts.summary: A code review of a bizarre C++ function submitted by a reader that reimplements a simple 'startsWith' check in a needlessly convoluted way. The function iterates character by character into a temporary string, then calls string::find on it — effectively doing what string::find could accomplish directly. The analysis points out that the while loop is redundant since the iterator is always rewound by the same number of characters regardless of outcome.

recent_posts.title: Java null check that always returns false
recent_posts.summary: A humorous code review post from The Daily WTF highlighting a Java anti-pattern where a method named `isNull` incorrectly wraps `StringUtils.isBlank`, and a follow-up method `isNullAndNull` that attempts to check for both blank values and the literal string "null" but uses `&&` instead of `||`, making it always return false.

recent_posts.title: How an AI agent deleted production and why everyone shares the blame
recent_posts.summary: A critical analysis of the PocketOS production deletion incident, where an AI agent (Claude via Cursor) deleted a production storage volume and its backups. The author dissects the multiple compounding failures: Railway's overly permissive tokens with no fine-grained scoping, storing API keys in source code, Railway's backup architecture that deletes backups with the volume, and the team disabling Cursor's safety guardrails. The author pushes back on the founder's framing that blamed only Cursor and Railway, arguing it was also a PocketOS failure of basic security hygiene, backup strategy, and tool understanding. The piece also critiques the anthropomorphization of LLM 'confessions' and emphasizes that AI agents are non-deterministic tools requiring strict supervision.

recent_posts.title: Misusing try/catch to handle a file dialog cancel in MATLAB
recent_posts.summary: A code review of a MATLAB snippet where a developer incorrectly uses a try/catch block to handle the cancel action from a file dialog (uigetfile). The function actually returns 0 on cancel rather than throwing an exception, so the catch block never fires, and the zero values propagate silently until something tries to open a file and crashes unexpectedly.

recent_posts.title: The risks of relying on a single whale client
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares a story about the dangers of over-relying on a single 'whale' client, illustrated by a company that spun up a dedicated server for one customer complaining about slow APIs — only to discover the real issue was unreliable mobile connectivity while driving. The author reflects on personal experiences with whale clients at two employers, including Facebook dictating support processes and Porsche monopolizing a startup's roadmap, arguing that diverse revenue streams are healthier than dependence on one dominant client.

recent_posts.title: Lint Brush Off
recent_posts.summary: A developer named Esben encountered a frustrating linter loop in C#: the linter complained about not using a primary constructor, so he added a pragma to suppress the warning. The linter then complained that the suppression was unnecessary. Attempting to suppress both warnings simultaneously failed because C# pragmas apply to the next line, ultimately requiring three lines of boilerplate just to silence a single stylistic suggestion.

recent_posts.title: April Showers
recent_posts.summary: A collection of reader-submitted software fails and IT absurdities: Reddit's API rejecting valid localhost IP URLs per RFC 1738/3986, a broken job posting form preventing resume submissions, a GM recall notification system sending emails for a car already at the dealer with wrong dealer location and fake phone numbers, a bank contact form that discourages contact, and TurboTax/Intuit displaying currency values with incorrect decimal formatting.

recent_posts.title: Why a static void method with no parameters is a refactoring red flag
recent_posts.summary: A short humorous code critique from The Daily WTF examining a C# static void method with no parameters and no return value. The method likely relies entirely on side effects — possibly manipulating a database or global state — making it difficult to test or debug. The post uses the example as a commentary on poor method design and the need for refactoring.

recent_posts.title: A Stack Overflow comment copy-pasted meaninglessly throughout a codebase
recent_posts.summary: A short humorous post from The Daily WTF highlighting a code smell: a Stack Overflow URL comment with no explanation, copied and pasted throughout an entire codebase delivered by an offshore team. The comment was originally relevant in one place but became meaningless noise everywhere else due to indiscriminate copy-pasting.

recent_posts.title: Turning Thirty
recent_posts.summary: A developer at a medical device company discovers a hard limit of thirty racks in a database and traces its origin through multiple generations of employees. The limit turns out to date back to 1986, when a developer constrained the database to fit on a single 5.25-inch floppy disk. Despite several ground-up rewrites over 40 years, each team blindly copied the constraint without ever questioning why it existed.

top_posts.title: Red flags at first job: a cautionary tale
top_posts.summary: Fresh out of university, Remco took a job abroad, ignoring his initial misgivings. Red flags about the company, Conglomcorp, started appearing early on, from concerning layoff practices to questionable software development practices like adding a misleading 'Garbage Collection' button that called System.gc(). Remco's experience worsened as he dealt with a poorly maintained codebase and unhelpful senior developers, leading him to eventually leave the company.

top_posts.title: The Modern Job Hunt: Part 1
top_posts.summary: A personal narrative about navigating the challenging modern job market, focusing on mental health strategies and reframing techniques to cope with job search stress. The story follows Ellis as she processes rejection and uncertainty by using cognitive reframing methods, viewing her job hunt as a search algorithm navigating obstacles, and finding meaning in the struggle through potential future writing about the experience.

top_posts.title: Navigating job search anxiety and rejection in 2025
top_posts.summary: A narrative about navigating the challenging 2025 job market follows Ellis through her emotional response to months of unsuccessful job applications. After attending a job hunting seminar, she uses cognitive reframing techniques from psychology books to combat anxiety and depression, viewing rejections as part of a search algorithm rather than personal failures. The piece shares coping strategies including recognizing emotions early, reframing negative thoughts, and finding meaning in the struggle by planning to help others through writing about the experience.

top_posts.title: Legacy system migration gone wrong with faulty field validation
top_posts.summary: A story about a poorly executed COBOL to RPG migration on an AS/400 system by a highly paid consultant. The migration resulted in buggy code that's still in production, including a field validation bug where numeric values stored as text are compared lexically instead of numerically, causing '21' < '5' to evaluate as true. The consultant blamed users for data discrepancies when reports didn't balance after migration.

top_posts.title: Router web interface breaks password managers with custom masking implementation
top_posts.summary: A router's web interface prevents password managers from working due to a custom password masking implementation that uses duplicate HTML IDs and JavaScript event interception instead of standard input type="password". The codebase exhibits numerous quality issues including duplicate jQuery libraries, unnecessary F5 key handling, bloated hexadecimal validation functions, and a password field that clears entirely when using backspace or arrow keys. These problems illustrate common issues in embedded device interfaces, often written by networking engineers without frontend expertise.
